notes:
Here are my verse-by-verse notes on Numbers 31:1–27, drawn from the sources I was able to retrieve.

---

## Numbers 31:1–27 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1: “And the LORD said to Moses…”

The chapter opens a new section: God initiates what follows. This is not Moses' idea or a human military campaign. The divine origin of the command is stressed repeatedly throughout the chapter. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-31/)

Matthew Henry notes this chapter belongs to “the book of the wars of the Lord” — it is the history of a holy war. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/numbers-31.html)

---

### v. 2: “Take vengeance on the Midianites for the Israelites. After that, you will be gathered to your people.”

**The command:** God orders vengeance (Hebrew *naqam*) on Midian. The Midianites were the nomadic people who, alongside Moab, had seduced Israel into sexual immorality and idolatry at Baal Peor (Numbers 25). God had already commanded hostility toward them in Numbers 25:16–17; now the time for execution has come. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-31/)

**“Vengeance”** — The Hebrew root *nqm* can also mean “vindication.” God's vengeance is not petty human revenge but righteous judgment against immorality and idolatry. Precept Austin notes that the combination of verb and noun (“take full vengeance” / “vengeance-vengeance”) emphasizes the necessity of full obedience. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-31-commentary)

**Why Midian and not Moab?** Matthew Poole (cited in Enduring Word) observes: “The Moabites also were guilty, but God out of his own good pleasure, and in kindness to Lot, was pleased to spare them, the rather, because the measure of their iniquity was not yet full.” Matthew Henry adds that God also spared Ammon for similar reasons (Deut. 2:8–9). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-31/) (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/numbers-31.html)

**Barnes:** “The war against the Midianites was no ordinary war. It was indeed less a war than the execution of a divine sentence against a most guilty people.” The sin was national, and retribution had to be national. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/numbers/31.htm)

**“Gathered to your people”** — Precept Austin examines this phrase at length. It is a euphemism for death but may imply more than burial. Walter Kaiser argues it reflects a genuine belief in an afterlife — being gathered to a community of believers who had gone before. The phrase is always distinguished from the act of burial in Scripture. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-31-commentary)

**Wiersbe** (cited in Precept Austin): This battle would be a “dress rehearsal” for the battles in Canaan. But it would be Moses' last battle; then he would meet “the last enemy” — death (1 Cor. 15:26). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-31-commentary)

---

### v. 3: “So Moses told the people, ‘Arm some of your men for war… to execute the LORD’s vengeance on them.’”

Moses promptly obeys. He calls it “the LORD’s vengeance” whereas God had said “vengeance for the Israelites.” The interests of God and Israel are one. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/numbers-31.html)

**Gill:** Moses spoke to the heads or princes of the tribes. According to Jewish writers, the men selected were “righteous men” who, detesting lewdness and idolatry, would more strictly avenge themselves on Midian for drawing their brethren into sin. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/31.htm)

**Precept Austin:** All sin is ultimately against Yahweh, and in this case Midian’s sin jeopardized the fulfillment of God’s covenant promises. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-31-commentary)

---

### v. 4: “Send into battle a thousand men from each tribe of Israel.”

A thousand from each tribe — 12,000 total. This was a small force compared to Israel’s 601,730 fighting-age men (Num. 26:51), and likely small compared to the Midianite enemy. **Gill:** “This was done to show that the war was of the Lord, he would fight the battle, and give them victory, it being the same to him to do it with few as with many.” The small number would encourage Israel to trust God against the more powerful enemies in Canaan. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/31.htm)

**Precept Austin** echoes this: “Who gets the glory when the numbers and human odds are aligned against us? God of course.” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-31-commentary)

---

### v. 5: “So a thousand men were recruited from each tribe of Israel—twelve thousand armed for war.”

The mustering from every tribe signified national unity. Every tribe had a stake in this holy war. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-31/)

---

### v. 6: “And Moses sent the thousand from each tribe into battle, along with Phinehas son of Eleazar the priest, who took with him the vessels of the sanctuary and the trumpets for signaling.”

**Phinehas** — the priest who had already shown zeal against Midianite seduction by spearing Cozbi and the Israelite man (Num. 25:7–8) — leads the campaign spiritually, not as a general. **Matthew Henry:** “He that had so well used the sword of justice against a particular criminal was best qualified to guide the sword of war against the whole nation.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/numbers-31.html)

**The holy articles/vessels:** Commentators debate what these were. **Wenham** (cited by Enduring Word): it could be the ark (cf. Josh. 6:6), the trumpets of alarm (Num. 10:1–10), or priestly garments (*keli* means “garment” in Deut. 22:5). Precept Austin argues the Ark may well have gone out, reasoning from Israel's first battle in Canaan (Josh. 6:13) where priests with trumpets accompanied the Ark. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-31/) (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-31-commentary)

**Clarke** (cited in Enduring Word): “Who then was general? Joshua, without doubt, though not here mentioned, because the battle being the Lord’s, he alone is to have the supreme direction, and all the glory.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-31/)

---

### v. 7: “Then they waged war against Midian, as the LORD had commanded Moses, and they killed every male.”

The phrase “as the LORD had commanded Moses” appears four times in this chapter (also vv. 31, 41, 47). The emphasis is that this was God’s battle. **Allen** (cited in Enduring Word): “killed every male” does not mean every single individual — it signals a complete military defeat with focus on enemy combatants. Some enemies fled; Midian reappears as an enemy later (Judges 6). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-31/)

**Precept Austin** notes a tension: the text says they acted “just as the LORD had commanded” — yet they spared the women, for which Moses later rebuked them. So their obedience was not yet complete. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-31-commentary)

---

### v. 8: “Among the slain were Evi, Rekem, Zur, Hur, and Reba—the five kings of Midian. They also killed Balaam son of Beor with the sword.”

**The five kings:** These are the same as “the elders of Midian” (Num. 22:4) and “the dukes of Sihon” (Josh. 13:21). **Zur** is of particular note — he was the father of Cozbi, the Midianite woman whom Phinehas slew (Num. 25:15). Cozbi was probably something of a Baal priestess, coming from such a powerful family. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-31/)

**Balaam:** His death here is theologically significant. He had counseled Midian to seduce Israel (Num. 31:16), doing so for money. **Enduring Word:** “Balaam, who had suggested the strategy to seduce Israel into sexual immorality and idolatry, and who did it all for money, was now dead.” This fulfills Jude 1:11 — the “error of Balaam for profit.” In Num. 23:10 Balaam wished to “die the death of the righteous,” but he had no interest in living the life of the righteous, so he died among God’s enemies. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-31/)

**Matthew Henry** surmises Balaam was there because the Midianites hired him again — this time to curse Israel’s army or bless Midian. Whatever brought him there, God’s providence placed him in the path of judgment. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/numbers-31.html)

**Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary:** “The soothsayer Balaam was slain in this battle, thus reaping the harvest of judgment for his complicity in seducing Israel.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/numbers-31.html)

---

### v. 9: “The Israelites captured the Midianite women and their children, and they plundered all their herds, flocks, and goods.”

According to the customs of ancient warfare, women and children were taken as captives/slaves, and all possessions became spoil. The Israelites followed standard practice. The problem — as Moses would soon point out — was that they spared the very women who had caused Israel’s downfall. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-31/)

---

### v. 10: “Then they burned all the cities where the Midianites had lived, as well as all their encampments.”

**Precept Austin:** Burning the cities eradicated all elements associated with Midianite idolatry — images, shrines, altars. Yet they spared the human carriers of that idolatry (the women). Israel later gave the Midianite territory to the tribe of Reuben (Josh. 13:15–23). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-31-commentary)

**Matthew Henry** suggests burning the cities prevented escapees from resettling — “not designing to inhabit them themselves (that country was out of their line).” Some understand it as burning idol-temples specifically. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/numbers-31.html)

---

### vv. 11–12: “They carried away all the plunder and spoils… to Moses, to Eleazar the priest, and to the congregation of Israel at the camp on the plains of Moab…”

The return to camp with captives and spoil sets the stage for Moses' confrontation. The location — plains of Moab by the Jordan across from Jericho — anchors this historically just before the conquest of Canaan. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-31/)

---

### v. 13: “And Moses, Eleazar the priest, and all the leaders of the congregation went to meet them outside the camp.”

**Matthew Henry:** Moses, despite his age, walked out of the camp to honor the returning soldiers. Public successes should be publicly acknowledged. But the meeting “outside the camp” also anticipates the purification requirement — they could not enter yet because of ceremonial defilement. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/numbers-31.html)

---

### v. 14: “But Moses was angry with the officers of the army… who were returning from the battle.”

Moses' anger was not severity for its own sake. **Morgan** (cited in Enduring Word): “Moses was wroth with the officers, not because of the severity of the judgment they had executed on Midian, but rather because they had failed to carry out the judgment completely.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-31/)

**Jamieson-Fausset-Brown:** “The displeasure of the great leader, though it appears the ebullition of a fierce and sanguinary temper, arose in reality from a pious and enlightened regard to the best interests of Israel.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/31-17.htm)

---

### v. 15: “Have you spared all the women?” he asked them.

A sharp rhetorical question expressing indignation. **Keil & Delitzsch** call it “an expression of dissatisfaction, and reproof for their having done this.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/31-17.htm)

**Enduring Word:** Moses was angry because the soldiers failed to see the spiritual danger. “God’s people may be deceived by things that were a threat, but do not seem to be a present danger. The Israelite officers of the army thought these women were safe, but they were more dangerous to Israel than an army of mighty warriors.” The greatest threats to God’s people are sometimes not military but moral and spiritual. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-31/)

---

### v. 16: “Look, these women caused the sons of Israel, through the counsel of Balaam, to turn unfaithfully against the LORD at Peor, so that the plague struck the congregation of the LORD.”

Here we learn explicitly that Balaam was the strategist behind the Midianite seduction — a fact not stated in Numbers 25 but confirmed here. **Barnes:** The women “became to the children of Israel for a cause (or, incitement) of treachery to the Lord.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/numbers/31.htm)

**Whedon's Commentary** (Methodist): “In the gradation of guilt Balaam, Balak, and the princes were first as contrivers of the nefarious scheme… and the women of Midian were second as the agents in its execution. Hence the indignant surprise of Moses that the latter had been spared.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/numbers-31.html)

**Benson** (Methodist): “Since the Moabites and their associates were taught by Balaam to acknowledge Jehovah to be a very powerful deity… is it not strange that they should have been induced, by Balaam’s persuasion, rather to entice the Israelites to their idolatry, than with them to embrace the worship of the true God?” Benson answers: these idolaters considered Jehovah not as the supreme God of the universe but as a mere local, tutelary deity of the Jews. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/numbers-31.html)

---

### v. 17: “So now, kill all the boys, as well as every woman who has had relations with a man.”

This is the most difficult verse in the chapter. The traditional readings offer several justifications:

**The women:** (a) Punishment — they had been guilty of sexual immorality and idolatry themselves and were confirmed in it beyond hope of reform. (b) Prevention — left alive, they would continue to seduce Israel. **Benson:** “Partly for punishment… and partly for prevention of the like mischief in future.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/31-17.htm)

**The boys:** (a) To exterminate the nation — the male line had to be cut off since a nation cannot be perpetuated through women alone (Keil & Delitzsch). (b) In that ancient culture, boys would grow up with a solemn duty to avenge their fathers and perpetuate Midianite culture and religion. **Enduring Word:** “This was harsh but done with the understanding that in that ancient culture, the boys would have grown into men with the solemn responsibility to avenge their fathers’ death.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-31/) (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/31-17.htm)

**Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary:** This was an act “both of justice and of mercy.” Justice because Midianite women had demonstrated their danger to Israel’s moral integrity. Mercy because it would have been cruel to leave defenseless women and children to starve in desolated cities with no protectors. Furthermore, Midianite boys left alive among Israelites “would grow up… and become a snare.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/numbers-31.html)

**Matthew Poole:** Normally Israel was forbidden to kill women and children (Deut. 20:14), but the Midianites had “equalled themselves” to the Canaanites “by their horrid crimes,” so God, “the supreme Lord of all men’s lives,” equaled them in punishment. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/31-17.htm)

**Clarke** (cited by Enduring Word): “For this action I account simply on the principle that God, who is the author and supporter of life, has a right to dispose of it when and how he thinks proper; and the Judge of all the earth can do nothing but what is right.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-31/)

**Matthew Henry’s Concise Commentary:** “The sword of war should spare women and children; but the sword of justice should know no distinction, but that of guilty or not guilty. This war was the execution of a righteous sentence upon a guilty nation, in which the women were the worst criminals.” It adds pastorally: “for children dying before actual sin, full provision is made as to their eternal happiness, by the mercy of God in Christ.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/31-17.htm)

---

### v. 18: “but spare for yourselves every girl who has never had relations with a man.”

**The young girls** were spared because: (a) they had not participated in the Baal Peor seduction, being virgins; (b) they were young enough to be brought into the covenant community and shaped by Israel's faith. **Cole** (cited by Enduring Word): “Only the young girls would be allowed to live so that they may be taken as wives or slaves by the Israelite men, according to the principles of holy war (Deuteronomy 20:13–14, 21:10–14). By this they could be brought under the umbrella of the covenant community of faith.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-31/)

**Trapp** (cited in Enduring Word): the determination “who have not known a man” was made “as far as they could conjecture by their age.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-31/)

**Whedon:** The pure maidens “could be incorporated into Israel without peril to the national religion. They could not be treated as concubines, since the law against fornication was in full force (Deut. 22:25–29), but they could be lawfully married to their captors (Deut. 21:10–14).” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/numbers-31.html)

**Gill:** They were kept “either to be handmaids to them, or to be married among them when grown up, and become proselytes, and initiated into their religion.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/31.htm)

---

### v. 19: “All of you who have killed a person or touched the dead are to remain outside the camp for seven days. On the third day and the seventh day you are to purify both yourselves and your captives.”

Even though the war was commanded by God, contact with death brought ceremonial uncleanness. **Wenham** (cited by Enduring Word): “Over every war, however glorious its outcome from the victor’s point of view, hangs the shadow of death. These purification rules reminded Israel that the death of one’s fellow men was a catastrophic disruption of God’s creation, even though in some cases it was the Creator himself who demanded the execution of the sinner.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-31/)

**Matthew Henry:** God would thus “preserve in their minds a dread and detestation of murder.” Even David could not build the temple because he had been a man of war (1 Chron. 28:3). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/numbers-31.html)

The third-day and seventh-day purification follows the pattern of the red heifer ceremony (Numbers 19). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-31-commentary)

---

### v. 20: “And purify every garment and leather good, everything made of goat’s hair, and every article of wood.”

All material spoil had been used by idolatrous Midianites and required ceremonial cleansing before use by the holy people. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-31/)

**Matthew Henry:** “These things had been used by Midianites, and, having now come into the possession of Israelites, it was fit that they should be sanctified to the service of that holy nation and the honour of their holy God. To us now every thing is sanctified by the word and prayer, if we are sanctified by the Spirit, who is compared both to fire and water.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/numbers-31.html)

---

### vv. 21–23: Eleazar’s instructions on fire and water purification.

Eleazar (not Moses) gives the specific ritual instructions, as these belong to the priestly domain. The principle: metals that can endure fire go through fire; everything else passes through water. After fire, items must still be purified with “the water of purification” — the water containing ashes of the red heifer (Numbers 19). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-31/)

**Meyer** (cited by Enduring Word): “The great aim of this enactment was to render these articles ceremonially clean. They had been in the use of the Midianites, and required cleansing, before they could be appropriated by Israel. But the cleansing processes were to be determined by their texture. Fire for what would stand fire; water for what could not stand fire.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-31/)

**Enduring Word** draws a typological application: fire pictures pressing difficulty (Job 23:10 — “When He has tested me, I shall come forth as gold”) and water pictures God’s Word (Eph. 5:26 — “washing of water by the word”). This is a charismatic/Pentecostal devotional reading. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-31/)

---

### v. 24: “On the seventh day you are to wash your clothes, and you will be clean. After that you may enter the camp.”

The seven-day waiting period ends with washing on the seventh day; then full re-entry into the camp and access to the tabernacle is restored. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-31/)

---

### v. 25: “The LORD said to Moses…”

A new divine speech introduces the instructions for dividing the spoil. God directs the division, preventing disputes. **Matthew Henry:** “It was fit that he who gave them the prey should order the disposal of it. All we have is from God, and therefore must be subject to his will.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/numbers-31.html)

---

### v. 26: “You and Eleazar the priest and the family heads of the congregation are to take a count of what was captured, both of man and beast.”

The inventory was supervised by Moses (civil authority), Eleazar (priestly authority), and the family heads (tribal authority) — ensuring transparency and fairness. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-31/)

---

### v. 27: “Then divide the captives between the troops who went out to battle and the rest of the congregation.”

This is an innovation. Customarily the spoil belonged entirely to the soldiers. Here God commands a 50/50 split between the 12,000 soldiers and the entire congregation (over 600,000). **Matthew Henry:** “Those that are employed in public trusts must not think to benefit themselves only by their toils and hazards, but must aim at the advantage of the community.” He notes that the individual soldier still got far more per person than any non-combatant — and “good reason they should.” David later made this a statute (1 Sam. 30:24–25). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/numbers-31.html)

---

## Denominational Distinctives & Other Views

### Methodist / Holiness (Benson, Whedon)

Both Benson and Whedon emphasize that Moses’ anger was neither personal nor excessive but arose from “pious and enlightened regard to the best interests of Israel.” Whedon carefully explains the gradation of guilt. Benson uniquely raises the theological conundrum: why did the Midianites not convert after Balaam showed them Jehovah’s superiority? His answer: they regarded Jehovah as merely a local tutelary deity. Neither source treats Numbers 31 as morally problematic — they accept it as righteous divine judgment. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/numbers-31.html) (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/numbers-31.html)

### Reformed / Presbyterian (Barnes, JFB, Keil & Delitzsch)

Barnes stresses divine sovereignty: “They had no discretion to kill or to spare… They had no alternative in this and similar matters except to fulfill the commands of God.” The slaughter is “an awful but doubtless salutary manifestation… of God's wrath against sin; and a type of the future extermination of sin and sinners from His kingdom.” JFB likewise anchors everything in the theocratic, holy-war character of the campaign. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/numbers/31.htm) (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/31-17.htm)

### Baptist (Gill, Garner-Howes)

Gill focuses on the details of selection — the “righteous men” chosen — and on the providence of God in using a small army. Garner-Howes uniquely frames the killing of women and boys as both justice and mercy: leaving them in desolated territory would have been crueler. Both treat the text as straightforward divine command. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/31.htm) (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/numbers-31.html)

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word — David Guzik)

Guzik reads the passage with strong application to spiritual warfare today. The Midianite women represent spiritual threats that do not look dangerous. The fire and water of purification typify the Holy Spirit’s refining and the Word’s cleansing. There is also emphasis on practical lessons about generosity (the officers gave far beyond the minimum) and on the new generation’s faithfulness compared to the generation that died in the wilderness. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-31/)

### Catholic (Haydock)

Haydock emphasizes that Moses did not reserve the girls “for the purpose of debauchery, as Paine ignorantly pretends; for that was contrary to his own laws.” He notes the boys were slain either because they would resent the injury or because they were all consecrated to Beelphegor — firstborn as priests, the rest as potential child sacrifices. Haydock insists the command was the “revenge of the Lord” (v. 3), and calls attention to the custom that women and children were ordinarily spared, but “the great lord of life and death was pleased to order it otherwise in the present case, in detestation of the wickedness of this people.” (From search excerpt at https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-31.html)

### Modern Scholarship / Critical View (Expositor's Bible, cited at StudyLight.org)

The Expositor’s Bible Commentary acknowledges that Wellhausen “roundly declared it to be fictitious” and that many have struggled with the passage. However, it dismisses the “Priests’ Code” invention theory: post-exilic ideas of purity in Ezra–Nehemiah would not have countenanced dedicating spared young girls as tribute to Jehovah. It concludes the account “must be held to stand” — a grim slaughter carried out at Moses’ command “in accordance with the moral and theocratic ideas that ruled his mind.” The passage then applies it spiritually: Christians must wage “relentless war against the vices and lusts with which too many are inclined to make terms.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/numbers-31.html)

---

**Note:** Due to search limits, I was unable to retrieve content directly from ligonier.org, desiringgod.org, thegospelcoalition.org, bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org, oca.org, or catholic.com for this passage. The denominational notes above are drawn from commentaries available through biblehub.com and studylight.org that represent those traditions (e.g., Barnes = Presbyterian, Gill = Reformed Baptist, Benson/Whedon = Methodist, Haydock = Catholic).
